title: What is the pyramid principle, and how does it make you sound clearer?
description: How to structure what you say so the listener gets the answer first, then the reasons, then the detail. With examples for cases and everyday work.
hook: Have you ever listened to someone explain something for two minutes before you understood what their point was? The pyramid principle is the cure. It is a simple idea, popularised by Barbara Minto, a former McKinsey consultant: say your main point first, then the few reasons that support it, then the detail. It is how consultants write and speak, and it will make you sound clearer in any interview.
body:
The shape

  • Top: the answer, in one sentence.
  • Middle: two to four reasons that support it.
  • Bottom: the facts and numbers behind each reason.

Bottom-up versus top-down

Most of us naturally speak bottom-up, telling the story in the order we discovered it: "First I looked at costs, then I noticed rent had grown, and then..." The listener has to wait to find out where you are going. Top-down flips it: "The profit fall is mostly rent. Two reasons..." The listener knows the point from the first sentence and can follow everything after it.

An example from a case

Bottom-up: "So I looked at the three regions, and the North was down 30%, while the South grew a bit, and the West was flat, and then within the North..."

Top-down: "The sales drop is almost entirely in the North. It fell 30% while the other regions held steady, and within the North, one large customer accounts for most of it."

Where to use it

  • Presenting your structure: "I'd look at three areas. First..."
  • After a chart or calculation: insight first, numbers second.
  • Your final recommendation: answer, reasons, risks, next steps.
  • Fit answers: one sentence on what the story shows, then the story.
  • Emails and messages at work: put the request or conclusion in the first line.

A small practice

Next time someone asks you a question today, try answering in one sentence first, then pause. If they want more, they will ask. You will be surprised how often the one sentence was enough.

Explain the answer in the order the listener needs it

Imagine your analysis shows that three underperforming stores explain nearly all of a chain's profit decline. A bottom-up answer starts with every store, month and spreadsheet tab. An answer-first version starts: "I recommend fixing or closing the three loss-making stores before expanding elsewhere." Then it gives the two most important reasons and the main condition or risk.

Make the reasons independently useful. "The stores are underperforming" merely repeats the conclusion. "They account for 85% of the decline" and "their rent contracts reset next quarter, so action is timely" are separate reasons grounded in evidence. Explain the numbers only after the listener understands why they matter.

Practise a 20-second and a 60-second version of the same recommendation. The short version should still name the decision and one decisive fact. The longer version can add trade-offs, uncertainty and next steps. If the interviewer interrupts after the opening sentence, your main message should already be clear.
